title: Even the wise drift (1 Kings 11:1–13)
hook: Solomon's heart turns in old age
carry: one small choice at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday, a queen came with chidot, hard questions. Your line was the half was not told. Today, the end of Solomon's story, and it turns.

A heart that hears. That's what Solomon asked for in a dream, at the very start. Since then he has judged between two mothers, built a house in quiet, prayed, saying heaven itself can't hold God, and asked that strangers be heard. A queen came to test him and went home amazed. Then the text turns a page and writes a sentence that begins, when Solomon was old. There's no single scene of falling. It's slower than that.
screen: `A HEART THAT HEARS.` → `JUDGE, BUILDER, PRAYER.` → `WHEN SOLOMON WAS OLD.`

segments.voice: The text says Solomon loved many foreign women, and gives the number itself: seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines. The Torah had warned that a king must not multiply wives, so that his heart not turn away. And verse four says just that, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods." He built high places for the gods of his wives' peoples, on the hill before Jerusalem. But the text doesn't let this be anyone else's fault. The LORD is angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned. His heart, the verse goes on, was not whole, in Hebrew not shalem, with God, as David's heart had been. The Talmud tells that Solomon reasoned he could take many wives and not be turned, and he was. His story opens with a heart, lev shomea, a listening heart. It closes with a heart that turned. Same heart. And there's no single moment of turning: the text lists marriages, then shrines for the gods of his wives, one after another. Nobody in the story wakes up one morning a different person. Many readers take Solomon's drift as a warning. The story doesn't call wisdom worthless; it shows that wisdom alone didn't keep him from turning. A king given wisdom in a dream still needed to keep choosing, every year, into old age. And the cost comes due in the next generation.
screen: `THE TORAH'S WARNING TO KINGS.` · `HIS HEART WAS NOT SHALEM.` · `A LISTENING HEART THAT TURNED.` · `ONE SMALL CHOICE, THEN ANOTHER.` · then, large: `WHEN SOLOMON WAS OLD.`

segments.voice: Is there something that matters to you that has slowly slipped, a habit of prayer, a friendship you used to tend, a value you once held tightly? With no scolding, trace it back to the small choice where the drift started, then name one small choice that could turn you back toward it. If you pray, you can ask for a whole heart.
Shalem. The Hebrew word for whole, the wholeness Solomon's heart lost toward God as he grew old. Today's word.

Your line: one small choice at a time. The week in lines: a listening heart, the real mother gives way, finished before anyone hears it, a place to turn toward, hear the stranger too, the half was not told, and this one. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's later years in the book of Kings, and the Talmud uses his story to show why the Torah's limits on a king matter even for the wise.

chat.says: How could someone as wise as Solomon end up turning away?
options: Wisdom alone didn't keep him; his heart turned slowly, one choice at a time.
A foreign army forced him to build the shrines against his will.
The prophets told him to build the shrines, to keep peace with his neighbors.
chat.meaning: The text names no single moment: when Solomon was old, his heart was not shalem, whole, after choice upon choice. Wisdom alone didn't keep him.

lev shomea.meaning: a listening heart, Solomon's first request

concubines.meaning: wives of lower rank in a royal household

Talmud.meaning: the rabbis' great record of law, debate and story

notes: The numbers (seven hundred wives, three hundred concubines) are stated in 1 Kings 11:3 and attributed to the text.
Sanhedrin 21b: Solomon said 'I will multiply and not turn aside', and turned. Confirm the citation.
The story must not read as blaming foreign women; the teach stresses the text's judgment falls on Solomon (11:9). Keeper to check tone.
